strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: prior LSNM causal discovery methods (LOCI, GRCI, QCCD) assume symmetric noise, and the paper convincingly demonstrates (Fig. 1, Fig. 3, Tables 4-5) that skewness induces misspecification and wrong causal inferences.

The choice of the skew-normal noise model is principled: it strictly generalizes the normal (λ=0) so it remains compatible with symmetric noise while covering a larger class, keeping the method within the identifiable LSNM class.

A non-trivial and novel estimation procedure is developed: a penalized spline-based skew-normal LSNM with a multi-stage estimator combining Bayesian optimization for penalty selection, CMA-ES heuristic search for initialization, and an ECM algorithm for refinement, with derivations of the Q-function and CM-steps.
The paper contributes novel synthetic benchmarks (ANs/LSs at three skewness levels using skew-normal and GNO noise) that will be useful to the community for evaluating robustness to skewness.

Empirical results on the skew-noise datasets are strong (SKEWD-LL reaches 100% accuracy across all skew levels), and the ablation (Tables 2-3) clearly demonstrates the necessity of the ECM refinement over the heuristic CMA-ES solution.
Limitations are discussed honestly, and the appendix provides the required technical detail (skew-normal/GNO properties, marginal-neglect argument, restated identifiability theorem).
weaknesses: The comparison against SOTA is weaker than the paper's framing suggests. On the 13 established benchmarks ROCHE outperforms both SKEWD variants (89.52% vs 87.46%/84.56%), and on the real-world Tübingen benchmark SKEWD-IT (66.57%) trails ROCHE (77.27%) by a wide margin. The claim of being 'on par with SOTA' and 'most reliable' is therefore only justified for the authors' own highly skewed synthetic data, not for real-world data.

The skew-noise benchmark appears comparatively easy and thus of limited discriminative power: IGCI-G, which the authors themselves call 'highly misspecified', makes only a single error across all six skew-noise datasets (Table 4). This raises questions about whether the benchmark actually isolates the difficulty of skewed noise or is largely solved by methods exploiting the near-injective/deterministic mechanisms.

There is an unexplained inconsistency between the model class and the results: the skew-normal distribution has maximum skewness ≈0.9953, yet SKEWD-LL achieves 100% on LSs(1.750) where the GNO noise has skewness ≈1.750, i.e., outside the representable range. The paper does not explain how/why the method still succeeds under this misspecification, leaving the robustness claim poorly understood.

The likelihood-scoring variant relies on the assumption that the marginal distributions of X and Y are (approximately) normal, justified only asymptotically via standardization. This is a strong assumption for real data and could bias the direction decision; the paper does not empirically test sensitivity to non-normal marginals.

No runtime or computational-cost analysis is provided, despite a pipeline involving Bayesian optimization with 8-fold CV, CMA-ES with population 100, and up to 5000 ECM iterations. Practical adoption and comparison to baselines (which use neural networks or simpler tests) requires such information.

Identifiability for the skew-normal LSNM is only asserted by reference to the general LSNM result; the specific PDE condition is not analyzed for the skew-normal parameterization, and boundary/non-identifiable cases (e.g., λ→0 interactions with the spline scale) are not characterized.
Presentation issues reduce clarity: inconsistent naming ('SkewD'/'SKEWD'/'SKEwD'), a typo in Appendix B ('CMA-ES-LL and CMA-ES-LL'), and several figures that are difficult to read at print size.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and under-explored problem: causal discovery in location-scale noise models when the noise distribution is skewed, which is common in real-world data.
Proposes a reasonable extension to skew-normal LSNMs and provides a detailed estimation procedure combining Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an ECM algorithm.
Offers two inference variants (independence testing and likelihood scoring) and evaluates them on synthetic skew datasets and established benchmarks.
The paper is generally well-written and well-structured, with clear motivation and informative figures.
Includes an ablation study showing the benefit of ECM refinement over the initial CMA-ES estimate.
Introduces novel synthetic datasets with controlled skewness levels, which could be useful for future research on robustness to skewness.
weaknesses: The likelihood scoring variant neglects marginal log-likelihoods based on the assumption that both X and Y are normally distributed after standardization. This assumption is violated in the skewed-noise setting (Y is skewed), making the likelihood score theoretically unsound. The proof in Appendix A only holds for normal marginals, so the core methodology is flawed.

The paper reports perfect accuracy (100%) on GNO(0,1,-0.5) datasets with skewness 1.750, which exceeds the maximum skewness (≈0.995) that the skew-normal distribution can represent. This is paradoxical and unexplained. It suggests either a bug in the experiments or that the method is exploiting an artifact rather than modeling skewness. The central claim of robustness under high skewness is therefore not convincingly supported.

Comparison to closely related work is insufficient. Lin et al. (2024) propose a skewness-based criterion for heteroscedastic noise and is highly relevant, but is not used as a baseline. Other recent methods (e.g., Sun & Schulte 2023) are also not compared.

On established benchmarks, SKEWD does not outperform the state of the art (ROCHE achieves 87.69% vs SKEWD-IT 85.02% and SKEWD-LL 77.43%). The claim of 'competitive' performance is weak, and the advantage is only on synthetic datasets that may favor the proposed model.

The computational cost is high: Bayesian optimization with 8-fold cross-validation, CMA-ES with population size 100 up to 5000 iterations, and ECM up to 5000 iterations per direction. No runtime or complexity analysis is provided, raising reproducibility and practicality concerns.
The method relies on several fixed hyperparameters (q=14, p=7, λ bounds, penalty ranges, number of folds) without sensitivity analysis. The robustness of the results to these choices is unknown.
No real-world skewed data is used to validate the method, despite the motivation citing real-world skewed examples (Genton 2004). The evaluation is limited to synthetic data and standard benchmarks.

The identifiability discussion relies on a general theorem for LSNMs but does not rigorously establish identifiability for the specific skew-normal LSNM, nor does it rule out the pathological cases for this parametric family.
The ECM algorithm uses CMA-ES for the second CM-step, which may break the monotonicity guarantee of ECM. No convergence diagnostics or discussion of local optima are provided.
The paper lacks a code repository or detailed reproducibility instructions, making it difficult for others to build on the work.

strengths: Addresses an important gap in causal discovery: prior LSNM methods predominantly assume symmetric noise, while real-world noise is often skewed. The proposed skew-normal LSNM generalizes the normal model and remains within the identifiable LSNM class.

Introduces a practical parameter estimation procedure combining Bayesian optimization for penalty parameters, CMA-ES for heuristic initialization, and an ECM algorithm for refinement. The ablation study shows the ECM step is critical (e.g., LSs(0.985) SKEWD-IT 82.5% vs. CMA-ES-IT 54.5%, Table 2).

Provides an extensive empirical evaluation: six novel skew-noise datasets with varying skewness levels, 13 established benchmarks including Tübingen, 11 baselines, and two inference variants. SKEWD-LL achieves perfect accuracy on all novel skew-noise datasets, and SKEWD-IT is competitive on established benchmarks (85.02% vs. ROCHE 87.69%, Table 1).

Clear presentation with informative illustrative examples (Fig. 1 and Fig. 3) showing how skewness induces residual dependence for LOCI and how SKEWD corrects it. The limitations and future work section is honest and useful.
weaknesses: The skew-normal distribution can only model skewness up to approximately 0.995, yet the paper claims robustness under high skewness and evaluates on GNO noise with skewness 1.750. In that setting, the model cannot represent the true noise skewness; the perfect accuracy of SKEWD-LL is not explained by skew-normal modeling, which weakens the central claim and raises concerns that the synthetic evaluation may not isolate the benefit of skewness modeling.

The likelihood scoring variant assumes standardized marginals are normal. This is a strong assumption that is often violated in real data. The paper acknowledges this, but SKEWD-LL underperforms SKEWD-IT on established benchmarks, limiting its practical applicability.

The ECM update equations appear to contain typos or ambiguities: in CM-step 1, the update for ψ uses \hat{ψ}^{(k)} instead of \hat{v}^{(k)} in the term (y − λ/(1+λ²) \hat{ψ}^{(k)}), and the λ update uses the old ψ rather than the updated ψ. As written, this is not a valid ECM step and could hinder reproducibility.

No code release or runtime/computational cost analysis is provided. The method requires expensive Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and ECM for every pair, which limits scalability and practical adoption. For example, Tübingen pair 69 required reduced ECM iterations due to its size.

Missing direct comparison to Lin et al. (2024), a related skewness-based causal discovery method mentioned in the related work. There are also no real-world experiments focused specifically on skewed noise beyond general benchmark datasets.

The novel synthetic datasets may be too easy or biased toward the proposed method: IGCI-G, a highly misspecified baseline, achieves near-perfect accuracy on the skew-noise datasets, suggesting that the evaluation may not fully isolate the contribution of explicit skewness modeling.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically important problem: existing LSNM-based causal discovery methods (LOCI, ROCHE, GRCI, QCCD) assume symmetric noise, and the paper convincingly demonstrates (Figure 1, Figure 2, Tables 5-6) that this misspecification degrades performance under skewness. This is a well-motivated gap.

Technically sound integration of the skew-normal distribution into the LSNM framework (Definition 3.1/3.3, Equation 3), with a carefully constructed estimation pipeline (Bayesian optimization for penalty parameters, CMA-ES initialization, and an ECM refinement adapted from Ferreira et al. 2023). The derivation of the penalized log-likelihood and the ECM E-step/CM-steps is coherent and grounded in established theory.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 19 bivariate benchmarks (6 novel skew-noise datasets plus 13 established ones) and multivariate experiments with d=6 and d=10, comparing against 8-11 SOTA baselines with both accuracy and AUDRC. Ablation studies (Tables 3-4 on the necessity of the ECM step, Tables 11-16 on KDE marginals) add useful insight.

The multivariate extension is more than window dressing: Proposition 5.1 (proof in Appendix A.4) formalizes that only nodes with unoriented edges need scoring, and the oracle-MEC variant (SkewD-MV-O) cleanly isolates estimation quality from PC-algorithm errors.

Strong performance where it matters: SkewD-LL achieves 100% accuracy across all skew-noise datasets including GNO cases with skewness 1.750 that exceed the skew-normal's theoretical range, and SkewD-IT/LL remain competitive on established benchmarks.

Good scholarly practice: honest limitations section, an impact statement flagging risks of incorrect causal conclusions under confounding, and detailed hyperparameter/implementation reporting in Appendix B.
weaknesses: The novel skew-noise benchmarks are generated directly from the model class SkewD assumes (skew-normal for two of three skewness levels). Perfect 100% accuracy on these datasets is suspicious and suggests the benchmark may be too easy or partially self-favoring; the paper does not report any baseline that also assumes skew-normal noise, so it is difficult to gauge how much of the gain is due to correct model class versus genuinely better inference.

The likelihood-scoring variant (SkewD-LL) rests on a Gaussian marginal assumption that is clearly violated in many real settings. The authors themselves show (Tables 13-14) that KDE marginals swing accuracy by up to 22% on SIM/SIMc/SIMIn/Tue, yet the main paper's claims rest on the Gaussian-marginal configuration. This makes the strong headline results fragile and dataset-dependent.

Computational cost is a serious practical concern that is under-reported. The bivariate method chains Bayesian optimization (8-fold CV) + CMA-ES (population 100, up to 5000 iterations, multiple starts) + ECM (up to 5000 iterations) per direction per pair, and the multivariate method scales with the number of parent-child configurations. No wall-clock runtimes or scaling plots are given, which limits reproducibility and adoption.

On established benchmarks the improvement is modest: SkewD-IT (85.02%) and SkewD-LL (77.43%) do not beat ROCHE (87.69%) in Table 1, and the paper's own framing ('performing on par with SOTA') concedes this. The contribution therefore hinges almost entirely on the novel skew benchmarks whose design is questioned above.

The multivariate results depend heavily on the PC algorithm: SkewD-MV-O (oracle MEC) is near-perfect while SkewD-MV drops to SHD 2.27/4.72, and the very poor baseline numbers (e.g., HOST SHD 21.21 at d=10) raise questions about whether baselines were fairly tuned. The paper does not diagnose this discrepancy.

Some presentation issues: the Q-function/v^2 equation block is garbled in the manuscript, and several references have inconsistent years (e.g., Blöbaum et al. listed as 2025 but cited as 2018; multiple entries appear misdated). These do not undermine the science but reflect insufficient copy-editing.

The paper claims robustness beyond the skew-normal's skewness bound (~0.9953) up to 1.750, but offers no mechanistic explanation for why the method extrapolates well. Without this, the claim of 'robustness under substantial deviations from the skew-normal assumption' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Identifiability is inherited from prior LSNM results (Immer et al., Strobl & Lasko) rather than re-derived for the skew-normal case, and Section 5.4 only restates these results. It is not verified that the specific skew-normal LSNM class satisfies the required PDE conditions in a non-trivial way.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation: existing LSNM methods (LOCI, ROCHE, GRCI, QCCD) assume symmetric noise, which is frequently violated in real data, and the paper clearly illustrates the resulting misspecification (Figure 1).

Provides a principled modeling extension: embedding the skew-normal distribution in the location-scale structural equation Y|X ~ SN(f(x), g(x), λ) with GAM/B-spline functions, and deriving a penalized-likelihood ECM procedure (adapted from Ferreira et al. 2023) with closed-form CM-steps is technically sound.

Strong and consistent empirical results on the proposed skew-noise benchmarks (SKEWD-LL reaches 100% accuracy across all skewness levels) and competitive results on established benchmarks, with the independence-test variant (SKEWD-IT) being robust across settings.

Contributes novel benchmark datasets with controlled skewness levels (ANs(γ1), LSs(γ1)) that could be useful to the community, plus a multivariate extension with a correct and useful Proposition 5.1 that restricts scoring to nodes with unoriented edges.
Clear writing and an honest limitations/impact discussion that acknowledges confounding, marginal misspecification, and scalability constraints.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is undermined by the benchmark itself: IGCI-G, which the authors describe as 'highly misspecified' and assuming almost-deterministic functions, makes only a single error across all skew-noise datasets (Table 5), nearly matching SKEWD-LL. This strongly suggests the proposed benchmark is easy to game (cf. Reisach et al. 2021), so it does not isolate the skewness challenge the paper claims to solve. The authors note this but do not investigate it.

The skew-noise datasets are largely generated with the same skew-normal distribution the method assumes (the λ = -2 and λ = 20 cases), so near-perfect accuracy is partly self-fulfilling; only the GNO cases probe out-of-model robustness.

Real-world performance is poor and contradicts the 'on par with SOTA' framing: SKEWD-LL attains only 45.97% on the Tübingen benchmark (below chance) and does not beat ROCHE on the established benchmarks (85.02% vs 87.69% accuracy; ROCHE is best overall at 89.52% vs SKEWD-LL 84.56% across 19 datasets). The headline likelihood variant thus has limited practical value.

The likelihood-scoring variants rely on a Gaussian marginal assumption, which is a strong and frequently violated requirement. The KDE ablation is mixed and the Tübingen result (45.97%) confirms this is a serious limitation rather than a minor caveat; SKEWD-LL is effectively restricted to near-Gaussian marginals.

The multivariate results hinge on MEC estimation: SKEWD-MV-O (oracle MEC) is near-perfect (SHD 0.14/0.04) while SKEWD-MV degrades sharply (SHD 2.27/4.72), and the baselines fail implausibly (HOST SHD 21.21, GraN-DAG++ 24.67 at d=10). The lack of investigation into why LSNM baselines collapse raises fairness/configuration concerns and makes it hard to attribute the gain to the method itself.

Computational cost is a major practical limitation: each fit requires Bayesian optimization over penalties, CMA-ES with population size 100 and up to 5000 iterations, plus ECM, repeated per direction and per admissible parent-child configuration. This is only briefly acknowledged and makes the method impractical for the 'moderately sized graphs' it targets.

The skew-normal has bounded skewness (~0.9953), yet the method reportedly succeeds on GNO data with skewness 1.750 that exceeds this range. This is asserted rather than explained, raising the question of whether the skew-normal assumption is actually the mechanism driving the improvement.

Novelty is incremental: the ECM algorithm is a modest adaptation of Ferreira et al. (2023) to the GAM/causal-discovery setting, and the primary new element is applying a known skewed distribution to LSNMs; no code or artifact link is provided, which limits reproducibility given the many hyperparameters.

strengths: Addresses a real and important gap: LSNMs with skewed noise are common, yet most existing LSNM methods assume symmetric noise. The skew-normal LSNM is a natural and useful extension that retains the Gaussian as a special case and inherits general LSNM identifiability results.

Provides a complete estimation pipeline: skew-normal LSNM formulation with GAMs/B-splines, penalized likelihood, Bayesian optimization for penalties, CMA-ES initialization, and an ECM algorithm adapted from Ferreira et al. (2023). Ablations show the ECM refinement substantially improves over heuristic estimates, especially for independence testing (e.g., LSs(0.985): 54.5% to 82.5%).

Extensive empirical evaluation: novel synthetic ANs/LSs datasets with controlled skewness (including GNO noise beyond skew-normal's skewness/kurtosis range), many LSNM/ANM/IGCI baselines, established benchmarks, and a multivariate extension. SKEWD-LL achieves 100% on all proposed skew-noise datasets; SKEWD-IT is competitive on established benchmarks.

Multivariate extension is a useful proof of concept: SKEWD-MV outperforms HOST, GraN-DAG++, and CAM on SHD/SID and precision/recall/F1 for d=6 and d=10, and SKEWD-MV-O demonstrates near-perfect orientation given a correct MEC.
The paper is generally transparent about limitations (identifiability, misspecification, KDE ablation, scalability) and includes an ethics/impact statement.

Originality is moderate but sufficient: while skew-normal noise modeling is a natural extension of LSNMs, adapting ECM to penalized GAM-based LSNMs, developing both independence- and likelihood-based variants, and constructing novel skew-noise benchmarks together constitute a useful novel contribution.
weaknesses: The likelihood-scoring variant (SKEWD-LL) assumes Gaussian marginals for both X and Y and neglects the marginal log-likelihoods. This assumption is violated on the skewed-noise datasets (Y is skewed), and the proof in Appendix A.3 only justifies the cancellation for Gaussian causes. The method's perfect performance on skewed data may rely on an unvalidated approximation; the KDE ablation shows marginal estimation matters but does not resolve the theoretical gap.

The novel skew-noise benchmark appears partially biased: IGCI-G, a method the authors describe as strongly misspecified and biased toward the correct direction, achieves near-perfect accuracy on the proposed datasets (e.g., 100% on ANs and almost all LSs, 99.5% on LSs(0.985)). This weakens the central empirical claim that skewness modeling is necessary to solve these benchmarks, since a non-skew-aware baseline nearly matches SKEWD-LL.

On the real-world Tübingen benchmark, SKEWD is not on par with SOTA: SKEWD-LL 45.97%, SKEWD-IT 66.57%, versus ROCHE 77.27%, GRCI 81.59%, QCCD 77.09%. The abstract/conclusion's 'on par with SOTA in other settings' overstates performance on real data and limits demonstrated practical utility.

The multivariate method is bottlenecked by the initial PC-based MEC estimation: SKEWD-MV-O with oracle MEC is near-perfect (SHD 0.14/0.04), while the full method has SHD 2.27/4.72. The paper does not analyze PC failures or compare to alternative MEC learners, so the source of remaining errors is not addressed. Scalability is also limited to small/dense graphs.

Reproducibility and computational practicality are insufficiently demonstrated: no code is provided, the pipeline is complex (Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, ECM, many hyperparameters), and no runtime or computational complexity comparisons are reported. This makes it difficult to assess practical cost and reproduce results exactly.

Presentation has several issues: garbled notation in the Q-function/v^2 definitions, duplicated 'CMA-ES-LL' in Table 3 caption, typos in proofs and text, and dense exposition. These do not invalidate the work but reduce clarity.
